pl-l4d17c1-d1e115.summary: Raises a manifold question: first, whether sin is forgiven by contrition of heart alone without satisfaction and confession of mouth; second, whether confessing to God without a priest ever suffices; third, whether confession made to a lay believer avails.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e118.summary: Notes that even the learned disagree, since the doctors seem to have taught various and almost contrary things.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e121.summary: Reports some who say no one is cleansed from sin without confession of mouth and satisfaction of work, if he had time to do them.
claims: Some hold confession and satisfaction necessary for remission.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e125.summary: Reports others who say sin is forgiven by God in contrition of heart, before confession and satisfaction, provided one intends to confess.
claims: Others hold contrition with intention to confess suffices for remission.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e128.summary: Cites the Psalm 'I said, I will confess my injustice to the Lord, and you forgave', with Cassiodorus: 'I said', that is, I resolved to confess, and you forgave; great is God's mercy, forgiving at the mere promise, since the vow is judged as the deed.
claims: God forgives at the resolution to confess.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e146.summary: Adds Augustine: he does not yet declare it but promises to, and God forgives, since saying this is a kind of declaring in the heart; there is not yet a voice in the mouth for man to hear the confession, but God hears.
claims: God hears the confession of the heart.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e155.summary: Adds further texts: 'a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God'; 'whenever the sinner turns and groans, he will live', not 'confesses with his mouth'; the lepers told to show themselves to the priests were cleansed on the way; Lazarus was raised within the tomb and came out alive, showing that the soul's raising precedes confession, since no one can confess unless raised, and no one is raised unless freed from sin.
claims: Remission can precede oral confession.
Confession presupposes the soul's being raised from sin.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e176.summary: Concludes that these and other texts prove that sin is forgiven by compunction alone, before confession or satisfaction.
claims: Compunction alone remits sin before confession.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e179.summary: Notes that those who deny this try to qualify these texts and cite authorities for their own opinion.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e183.summary: Gives their first authority, Isaiah: 'tell your iniquities, that you may be justified'.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e189.summary: Gives Ambrose: no one can be justified from sin unless he first confesses it.
claims: Confession is necessary for justification.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e198.summary: Gives Ambrose: confession frees the soul from death, opens paradise, gives hope of salvation, since one who will not confess in life does not merit justification; the confession that frees is that made with penance, which is grief of heart for evils done.
claims: Confession with penance frees from death.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e204.summary: Gives John (Chrysostom): no one can receive God's grace unless purged of all sin by the confession of penance and by baptism.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e210.summary: Gives Augustine: do penance as it is done in the Church; let no one say 'I do it secretly, before God; God who forgives knows I do it in my heart'. Was 'whatever you loose on earth' said in vain? Were the keys given in vain? We frustrate Christ's word.
claims: Secret penance alone frustrates the keys.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e225.summary: Gives Ambrose: the fault followed by confession of offenses is pardonable.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e235.summary: Gives Augustine on 'let not the pit close its mouth over me': the pit of iniquity will not close over you if you do not close your mouth; confess and you will escape; it closes over one who despises in the depths, from whom, as dead, confession perishes.
claims: Confession keeps the pit from closing.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e256.summary: Gives Augustine: no one receives pardon of a graver penalty owed unless he pays some penalty, though far less than owed; God's generous mercy does not abandon the justice of discipline.
claims: Pardon requires some penalty paid.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e262.summary: Gives Jerome: let the sinner lament his own and the people's offenses, enter the Church he left through sins, and sleep in sackcloth, to compensate past pleasures by austerity.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e271.summary: Notes that on these and many other authorities they assert that no one is cleansed from sin without oral confession and some payment of penalty.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e274.summary: Asks what is to be thought and held about this.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e277.summary: Answers that sins are blotted out by contrition and humility of heart without oral confession and outward penalty: from the moment one resolves with compunction to confess, God forgives, since there is confession of the heart, though not of the mouth, by which the soul is inwardly cleansed of the stain and contagion of sin and the debt of eternal death is remitted.
claims: Contrition with the resolution to confess remits sin.
It cleanses the stain and remits eternal death.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e281.summary: Interprets the opposing authorities: they refer either to confession of heart and inward punishment, as Augustine's saying that no one gains pardon without paying some penalty; or to outward penalty and to those who despise or neglect it, as 'let no one say: I do it secretly'; for some neglect or are ashamed to confess and so do not merit justification.
claims: The opposed texts concern inward penance or those who despise confession.

pl-l4d17c1-d1e290.summary: Adds that as inward penance is commanded, so are oral confession and outward satisfaction if possible; so one who lacks the intention to confess is not truly penitent. As remission is God's gift, so penance and confession, by which sin is deleted, can only be from God; Augustine: one who confesses and repents already has the Spirit's gift, since one cannot of himself be angry with and displeased at himself. The penitent must confess if he has time; yet before confession is in the mouth, if the intention is in the heart, remission is granted.
claims: Oral confession and satisfaction are commanded if possible.
Without intention to confess there is no true penance.
Penance and confession are gifts of the Spirit.

pl-l4d17c1.summary: Raises three questions: whether sin is forgiven by contrition alone, without confession and satisfaction; whether confessing to God alone suffices; and whether confession to a lay believer avails. On the first, some say no one is cleansed without confession and satisfaction if there is time; others that sin is forgiven in contrition before confession if one intends to confess, citing the Psalm ('I said I will confess, and you forgave'), Cassiodorus, Augustine, the lepers cleansed on the way, and Lazarus raised before coming out. The first group cite Isaiah, Ambrose, Augustine ('say not: I do it secretly before God; else the keys were given in vain'), and Jerome. Lombard holds that sins are blotted out by contrition and humility of heart, without confession of mouth and outward satisfaction, once one intends to confess: this is the confession of the heart, which cleanses the stain and remits eternal death. The opposed texts concern inward confession and punishment, or those who neglect or despise outward confession. Yet confession and satisfaction are commanded if possible, and one who lacks the intention to confess is not truly penitent; both penance and confession are gifts of the Spirit.
claims: Some hold no one is cleansed without confession and satisfaction; others that contrition with the intention to confess suffices.
Sin is forgiven by contrition with the intention of confessing, before oral confession.
Contrition remits the stain and eternal death.
Oral confession and satisfaction are still required when possible.
One without the intention to confess is not truly penitent.
Penance and confession are gifts of the Holy Spirit.
